chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: On the evening of September 1, after his meeting with Kutuzov, Count Rostopchin had returned to Moscow feeling humiliated and offended — because he hadn't been invited to the council of war, and because Kutuzov had paid no attention to his offer to help defend the city. He was also stunned by the new perspective revealed at camp, where the capital's peace of mind and patriotic fervor were treated as not merely secondary but entirely irrelevant. Hurt, offended, and bewildered, Rostopchin returned to Moscow. After supper he lay down on the sofa without undressing and was woken soon after midnight by a courier bringing a letter from Kutuzov. The letter requested the count to send police officers to guide troops through the city, as the army was retreating to the Ryazan road beyond Moscow. This was not news to Rostopchin. He had known Moscow would be abandoned not merely since his meeting with Kutuzov on Poklonny Hill the previous day, but ever since the Battle of Borodino — every general who came to Moscow after that battle unanimously declared it impossible to fight again, and since then government property had been removed every night and half the inhabitants had left with Rostopchin's own permission. Yet this information astonished and irritated the count, coming as a simple note with an order from Kutuzov, received in the middle of the night, breaking into his sleep.

When later, in his memoirs, Count Rostopchin explained his actions during this period, he repeatedly claimed to have been guided by two important aims: maintaining calm in Moscow and speeding the departure of its residents. If one accepts this dual aim, all of Rostopchin's actions appear beyond reproach. "Why were the holy relics, the weapons, ammunition, gunpowder, and grain supplies not removed? Why were thousands of inhabitants deceived into thinking Moscow wouldn't be surrendered — and thereby ruined?" "To preserve the city's calm," explains Count Rostopchin. "Why were bundles of useless papers from government offices, and Leppich's balloon and other items, removed?" "To leave the city empty," explains Count Rostopchin. One need only accept that public order is threatened, and any action can be justified.
All the horrors of the Reign of Terror were based on nothing but concern for public order.

On what, then, was Rostopchin's fear for Moscow's order based in 1812? What reason was there to expect an uprising? The residents were leaving and the retreating troops were filling the city. Why would the masses riot?

Neither in Moscow nor anywhere else in Russia did anything resembling an insurrection ever occur when the enemy entered a city. More than ten thousand people still remained in Moscow on September 1 and 2, and except for a mob in the governor's courtyard — assembled there at his own invitation — nothing happened. It is obvious that there would have been even less cause for unrest if, after the Battle of Borodino, when Moscow's surrender became certain or at least probable, Rostopchin — instead of stirring up the people by distributing weapons and broadsheets — had taken steps to remove the holy relics, the gunpowder, munitions, and money, and had plainly told the population that the city would be given up.

Rostopchin, though he had patriotic feelings, was an impulsive, hot-blooded man who had always moved in the highest administrative circles and had no understanding at all of the people he imagined he was guiding. Ever since the enemy entered Smolensk, he had been playing — in his own mind — the role of director of popular feeling in "the heart of Russia." Not only did he believe (as all administrators do) that he controlled the external actions of Moscow's residents, but he also thought he shaped their inner attitudes through his broadsheets and posters, written in a coarse style that the common people despise in their own kind and don't understand coming from those in authority. Rostopchin was so pleased with his fine role as leader of popular feeling, and had grown so accustomed to it, that the need to give it up and abandon Moscow without any heroic display caught him completely off guard. The ground slipped from under his feet, and he had no idea what to do. Though he knew it was coming, he didn't truly believe until the last moment that Moscow would be abandoned, and he made no preparations. The residents left against his wishes. If government offices were evacuated, it was only at the insistence of the officials, whom the count reluctantly obliged. He was absorbed in the role he had created for himself. As often happens with those gifted with vivid imaginations, though he had long known Moscow would be abandoned, he knew it only with his intellect — not in his heart — and did not mentally adapt to this new reality.

All his painstaking and energetic activity (whether it was useful or had any effect on the people is another question) had been aimed simply at arousing in the masses his own feeling of patriotic hatred for the French.

But when events assumed their true historical character — when expressing hatred for the French in words proved insufficient, when it wasn't even possible to express that hatred by fighting a battle, when self-confidence was of no use against the one question facing Moscow, when the entire population streamed out as one man, abandoning their property and thereby demonstrating through this negative act all the depth of their national feeling — then the role Rostopchin had chosen suddenly appeared senseless. He found himself suddenly ridiculous, weak, and alone, with no ground to stand on.

When, roused from sleep, he received that cold, peremptory note from Kutuzov, he felt all the more enraged because he felt he was to blame. Everything that had been specifically entrusted to him — the state property that should have been evacuated — was still in Moscow, and it was no longer possible to remove it all.

"Who is to blame? Who let things come to this?" he brooded. "Not me, of course. I had everything ready. I had Moscow firmly in hand. And this is what they've let it come to! Villains! Traitors!" he thought — without clearly identifying who the villains and traitors were, but feeling an urgent need to hate these people, whoever they were, who were responsible for the false and absurd position in which he found himself.
All that night Count Rostopchin issued orders, and people came to him from every part of Moscow. Those around him had never seen the count so grim and irritable.

"Your excellency, the Director of the Registrar's Department has sent for instructions... From the Consistory, from the Senate, from the University, from the Foundling Hospital, the Suffragan has sent... asking for orders... What are your instructions about the Fire Brigade? From the prison governor... from the superintendent of the lunatic asylum..." All night long such reports kept coming in.

To all these inquiries he gave short, angry replies indicating that his instructions were no longer needed, that the entire plan he had carefully prepared had been ruined by someone else, and that someone else would have to bear responsibility for everything that followed.

"Oh, tell that blockhead," he said in reply to the inquiry from the Registrar's Department, "that he should stay and guard his documents. Now why are you asking stupid questions about the Fire Brigade? They've got horses — let them go to Vladimir and not leave them to the French."
"Your excellency, the superintendent of the lunatic asylum has come. What are your orders?"
"My orders? Let them all go — that's all. And let the lunatics loose in the city. When madmen are commanding our armies, God obviously wants these other madmen to be free."
In reply to a question about the convicts in the prison, Count Rostopchin shouted angrily at the governor:
"Do you expect me to provide two battalions — which we don't have — as a convoy? Release them, and that's the end of it!"
"Your excellency, there are some political prisoners — Meshkov, Vereshchagin..."
"Vereshchagin! Hasn't he been hanged yet?" Rostopchin shouted. "Bring him to me!"

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: By around nine o'clock in the morning, when the troops were already marching through Moscow, nobody came to the count for instructions anymore. Those who could get away were leaving on their own, and those who stayed behind decided for themselves what they had to do.
The count ordered his carriage so he could drive to Sokolniki, and sat in his study with his hands folded, gloomy, sallow-faced, and silent.

In quiet, untroubled times, every administrator imagines that the entire population under his rule is kept going only by his efforts, and it is this sense of being indispensable that provides the chief reward for his labor. While the sea of history remains calm, the ruler-administrator in his little boat, holding on with a boat hook to the great ship of the people and moving along with it, naturally imagines that his efforts are moving the ship. But as soon as a storm arises and the sea begins to heave, such a delusion becomes impossible. The ship moves on its own with its own enormous force, the boat hook no longer reaches the vessel, and suddenly the administrator—instead of appearing a powerful ruler—becomes an insignificant, useless, feeble man.
Rostopchin felt this, and it was what enraged him.

The superintendent of police, who had been stopped by the crowd, came to see him at the same time as an adjutant who informed the count that the horses were harnessed. They were both pale, and the superintendent, after reporting that he had carried out his instructions, informed the count that a huge crowd had gathered in the courtyard and wanted to see him.

Without saying a word, Rostopchin rose and walked quickly to his elegant, luxurious drawing room, went to the balcony door, took hold of the handle, let it go again, and went to the window from which he could better see the whole crowd. The tall young man was standing in front, waving his arm and saying something with a stern expression. The blood-stained blacksmith stood beside him looking gloomy. A hum of voices could be heard through the closed window.
"Is my carriage ready?" asked Rostopchin, stepping back from the window.
"It is, your excellency," replied the adjutant.
Rostopchin went again to the balcony door.
"But what do they want?" he asked the superintendent of police.

"Your excellency, they say they've gotten ready, according to your orders, to go fight the French, and they shouted something about treachery. But it's a rowdy crowd, your excellency—I barely managed to get away from them. Your excellency, I'd suggest..."
"You can go. I don't need you to tell me what to do!" Rostopchin snapped angrily.
He stood by the balcony door looking at the crowd.

"This is what they've done with Russia! This is what they've done with me!" he thought, full of an irrepressible fury welling up inside him against someone to whom all of this could be blamed. As often happens with passionate people, he was consumed by anger but was still looking for a target to vent it on. "There's that mob, the dregs of the people," he thought, gazing at the crowd: "this rabble they've stirred up with their stupidity! They want a victim," he thought, looking at the tall young man waving his arm. And this thought came to him precisely because he himself wanted a victim, something on which to vent his rage.
"Is the carriage ready?" he asked again.
"Yes, your excellency. What are your orders about Vereshchagin? He's waiting at the entrance," said the adjutant.
"Ah!" exclaimed Rostopchin, as if struck by an unexpected memory.
And opening the door quickly, he walked out resolutely onto the balcony. The talking instantly stopped, hats and caps came off, and all eyes were raised to the count.

"Good morning, lads!" said the count briskly and loudly. "Thank you for coming. I'll come out to you in a moment, but first we must deal with the villain. We must punish the villain who has caused the ruin of Moscow. Wait for me!"
And the count stepped just as briskly back inside and slammed the door behind him.

A murmur of approval and satisfaction ran through the crowd. "He'll deal with all the villains, you'll see! And you said the French... He'll show you what law is!" the mob was saying, as if reproaching one another for their lack of confidence.

A few minutes later an officer came hurrying out of the front door, gave an order, and the dragoons formed a line. The crowd moved eagerly from the balcony toward the entrance. Rostopchin, coming out there with quick, angry steps, looked hastily around as if searching for someone.

"Where is he?" he asked. And as he spoke, he saw a young man being led around the corner of the house between two dragoons. He had a long thin neck, and his head, which had been half shaved, was again covered with short hair. This young man wore a threadbare blue cloth coat lined with fox fur that had once been elegant, and dirty prison trousers. On his thin, weak legs were heavy chains that hampered his uncertain steps.
"Ah!" said Rostopchin, hurriedly looking away from the young man in the fur-lined coat and pointing to the bottom step of the entrance. "Put him there."

The young man, his chains clanking, stepped clumsily to the spot indicated, holding away with one finger the coat collar that chafed his neck. He turned his long neck this way and that, sighed, and submissively folded his thin hands—hands unused to labor—in front of him.

For several seconds while the young man was taking his place on the step, silence held. Only among the back rows of the people pressing toward the same spot could sighs, groans, and the shuffling of feet be heard.
While waiting for the young man to settle on the step, Rostopchin stood frowning and rubbing his face with his hand.
"Lads!" he said, with a metallic ring in his voice. "This man, Vereshchagin, is the scoundrel who has brought ruin on Moscow."

The young man in the fur-lined coat, stooping slightly, stood in a submissive posture with his fingers clasped before him. His emaciated young face, disfigured by the half-shaven head, hung down hopelessly. At the count's first words he slowly raised it and looked up at him as if wanting to say something, or at least to meet his eyes. But Rostopchin did not look at him. A vein in the young man's long thin neck swelled like a cord and turned blue behind his ear, and suddenly his face flushed.

All eyes were fixed on him. He looked at the crowd, and made somewhat hopeful by the expressions he read on those faces, he smiled sadly and shyly, and lowered his head, shifting his feet on the step.

"He has betrayed his Tsar and his country. He has gone over to Bonaparte. He alone of all Russians has disgraced the Russian name. He has caused Moscow to perish," said Rostopchin in a sharp, even voice, but suddenly he glanced down at Vereshchagin, who continued to stand in the same submissive pose. As if inflamed by the sight, he raised his arm and addressed the people, almost shouting:
"Deal with him as you see fit! I hand him over to you."

The crowd remained silent and only pressed closer and closer together. To hold one another back, to breathe in that stifling atmosphere, to be unable to move, and to await something unknown, incomprehensible, and terrible was becoming unbearable. Those standing in front, who had seen and heard what was happening, all stood with wide-open eyes and mouths, straining with all their strength, holding back the crowd that pushed behind them.
"Beat him! Let the traitor die and not disgrace the Russian name!" shouted Rostopchin. "Cut him down! I command it!"
Hearing not so much the words as the angry tone of Rostopchin's voice, the crowd groaned and surged forward, but stopped again.

"Count!" cried the timid yet dramatic voice of Vereshchagin in the momentary silence that followed. "Count! One God is above us both..." He lifted his head and again the thick vein in his thin neck filled with blood as the color rapidly came and went in his face.
He did not finish what he wanted to say.
"Cut him down! I command it..." shouted Rostopchin, suddenly growing pale like Vereshchagin.
"Draw sabers!" cried the dragoon officer, drawing his own.

Another still stronger wave flowed through the crowd and reaching the front ranks carried it swaying to the very steps of the entrance. The tall youth, with a stony look on his face and a rigid, uplifted arm, stood beside Vereshchagin.
"Saber him!" the dragoon officer almost whispered.
And one of the soldiers, his face suddenly distorted with fury, struck Vereshchagin on the head with the blunt side of his saber.

"Ah!" cried Vereshchagin in meek surprise, looking around with a frightened expression as if not understanding why this was being done to him. A similar gasp of surprise and horror ran through the crowd. "O Lord!" exclaimed a sorrowful voice.

But after the exclamation of surprise that had escaped from Vereshchagin, he uttered a cry of pain, and that cry was fatal. The barrier of human feeling, strained to its utmost, that had held the crowd in check suddenly broke. The crime had begun and had to be completed. The plaintive moan of reproach was drowned by the threatening, angry roar of the crowd. Like the seventh and last wave that shatters a ship, that final irresistible wave burst from the rear and reached the front ranks, sweeping them off their feet and engulfing them all. The dragoon was about to repeat his blow. Vereshchagin, crying out in horror and covering his head with his hands, rushed toward the crowd. The tall youth, against whom he stumbled, seized his thin neck with his hands and, yelling wildly, fell with him under the feet of the pressing, struggling crowd.

Some beat and tore at Vereshchagin, others at the tall youth. And the screams of those being trampled and of those who tried to rescue the tall lad only increased the fury of the crowd. It was a long time before the dragoons could pull out the bleeding youth, beaten almost to death. And for a long time, despite the feverish haste with which the mob tried to finish the work it had begun, those who were hitting, strangling, and tearing at Vereshchagin could not kill him, because the crowd pressed from all sides, swaying as one mass with them in the center, making it impossible either to kill him or let him go.
"Hit him with an ax, eh!... Crushed?... Traitor, he sold Christ... Still alive... stubborn... serves him right! Torture serves a thief right. Use the hatchet!... What—still alive?"

Only when the victim ceased to struggle and his cries changed to a long, measured death rattle did the crowd around his prostrate, bleeding corpse begin rapidly to change places. Each person came up, glanced at what had been done, and with horror, reproach, and astonishment pushed back again.

"O Lord! The people are like wild beasts! How could he still be alive?" voices in the crowd could be heard saying. "Quite a young fellow too... must have been a merchant's son. What men!... and they say he's not the right one... How not the right one?... O Lord! And there's another one who's been beaten too—they say he's nearly done for... Oh, the people... Aren't they afraid of sinning?..." said the same mob now, looking with pained distress at the dead body with its long, thin, half-severed neck and its livid face stained with blood and dust.

A careful police officer, finding the presence of a corpse in his excellency's courtyard unseemly, told the dragoons to take it away. Two dragoons grabbed it by its distorted legs and dragged it along the ground. The gory, dust-stained, half-shaven head with its long neck trailed twisting along the ground. The crowd shrank back from it.

At the moment Vereshchagin fell and the crowd closed in with savage yells, Rostopchin suddenly turned pale and, instead of going to the back entrance where his carriage was waiting, hurried with bent head along the corridor leading to the rooms on the ground floor, not knowing where he was going or why. The count's face was white and he could not control the feverish twitching of his lower jaw.
"This way, your excellency... Where are you going?... This way, please..." said a trembling, frightened voice behind him.

Count Rostopchin was unable to reply and, turning obediently, went in the direction indicated. At the back entrance stood his carriage. The distant roar of the yelling crowd was audible even there. He hastily got in and told the coachman to drive him to his country house in Sokolniki.

When they reached Myasnitsky Street and could no longer hear the shouts of the mob, the count began to feel remorse. He remembered with dissatisfaction the agitation and fear he had shown before his subordinates. "The mob is terrible—disgusting," he said to himself in French. "They are like wolves that only flesh can satisfy." "Count! One God is above us both!"—Vereshchagin's words suddenly came back to him, and an unpleasant shiver ran down his back. But this was only a momentary feeling, and Count Rostopchin smiled scornfully at himself. "I had other duties," he thought. "The people had to be calmed. Many other victims have perished and are perishing for the public good"—and he began thinking of his social duties to his family and to the city entrusted to him, and of himself—not himself as Theodore Vasilyevich Rostopchin (he imagined that Theodore Vasilyevich Rostopchin was sacrificing himself for the public good) but himself as governor, the representative of authority and of the Tsar. "Had I been simply Theodore Vasilyevich, my course of action would have been quite different, but it was my duty to safeguard my life and dignity as commander in chief."

Gently swaying on the flexible springs of his carriage and no longer hearing the terrible sounds of the crowd, Rostopchin grew physically calm and, as always happens, as soon as he became physically calm his mind found reasons why he should be mentally calm too. The thought that calmed Rostopchin was not a new one. Since the world began and men have killed one another, no one has ever committed such a crime against a fellow human without comforting himself with this same idea. This idea is the public good—the hypothetical welfare of other people.
For a person not driven by passion, that welfare is never certain, but the one who commits such a crime always knows exactly where that welfare lies. And Rostopchin now knew it.

Not only did his reason not reproach him for what he had done, but he even found cause for satisfaction in having so successfully seized a convenient opportunity to punish a criminal while also pacifying the mob.

"Vereshchagin was tried and condemned to death," thought Rostopchin (though the Senate had only sentenced Vereshchagin to hard labor). "He was a traitor and a spy. I could not let him go unpunished, and so I killed two birds with one stone: I gave the mob a victim to calm them, and I punished a criminal."
Having reached his country house and begun giving orders about household arrangements, the count grew quite calm.

Half an hour later he was driving with fast horses across the Sokolniki field, no longer thinking of what had happened but considering what was still to come. He was heading to the Yauza bridge, where he had heard that Kutuzov was. Count Rostopchin was mentally preparing the angry, stinging reproaches he intended to deliver to Kutuzov for his deception. He would make that sly old courtier feel that the responsibility for all the calamities following the abandonment of the city and the ruin of Russia (as Rostopchin saw it) would fall on his senile old head. Planning what he would say to Kutuzov, Rostopchin angrily turned in his carriage and gazed sternly from side to side.

The Sokolniki field was deserted. Only at the far end, in front of the almshouse and the lunatic asylum, could some people in white be seen, and others like them walking alone across the field, shouting and gesturing.

One of these was running to cross the path of Count Rostopchin's carriage, and the count himself, his coachman, and his dragoons all looked with vague horror and curiosity at these released lunatics, especially at the one running toward them.

Swaying from side to side on his long, thin legs in his fluttering dressing gown, this madman was running straight at Rostopchin, shouting something in a hoarse voice and making signs for him to stop. The lunatic's solemn, gloomy face was thin and yellow, with its beard growing in uneven tufts. His black pupils with saffron-yellow whites moved restlessly near the lower eyelids.
"Stop! Pull up, I tell you!" he cried in a piercing voice, and again shouted something breathlessly with emphatic gestures.
Coming alongside the carriage, he ran beside it.

"Three times have they slain me, three times have I risen from the dead. They stoned me, crucified me... I shall rise... shall rise... shall rise. They have torn my body. The kingdom of God will be overthrown... Three times will I overthrow it and three times re-establish it!" he cried, raising his voice higher and higher.

Count Rostopchin suddenly grew pale as he had done when the crowd closed in on Vereshchagin. He turned away. "Go fas... faster!" he cried in a trembling voice to his coachman. The carriage flew over the ground as fast as the horses could pull it, but for a long time Count Rostopchin still heard the insane, despairing screams growing fainter in the distance, while his eyes saw nothing but the astonished, frightened, bloodstained face of "the traitor" in the fur-lined coat.

Recent as that image was, Rostopchin already felt that it had cut deep into his heart and drawn blood. Even now he felt clearly that the bloody trace of that memory would not fade with time, but that the terrible recollection would, on the contrary, dwell in his heart ever more cruelly and painfully to the end of his life. He seemed still to hear the sound of his own words: "Cut him down! I command it..."

"Why did I say those words? It was by some accident I said them... I didn't need to say them," he thought. "And then nothing would have happened." He saw the frightened and then furious face of the dragoon who dealt the blow, the look of silent, timid reproach that boy in the fur-lined coat had turned upon him. "But I didn't do it for my own sake. I was obligated to act that way... The mob, the traitor... the public welfare," thought he.

Troops were still crowding at the Yauza bridge. It was hot. Kutuzov, dejected and frowning, sat on a bench by the bridge toying with his riding whip in the sand when a carriage dashed up noisily. A man in a general's uniform with plumes in his hat went up to Kutuzov and said something in French. It was Count Rostopchin. He told Kutuzov that he had come because Moscow, the capital, was no more and only the army remained.
"Things would have been different if your Serene Highness had not told me that you would not abandon Moscow without another battle; all this would not have happened," he said.

Kutuzov looked at Rostopchin as if, not grasping what was being said to him, he was trying to read something peculiar written at that moment on the face of the man addressing him. Rostopchin grew confused and fell silent. Kutuzov slightly shook his head and, without taking his penetrating gaze from Rostopchin's face, muttered softly:
"No! I shall not give up Moscow without a battle!"

Whether Kutuzov was thinking of something entirely different when he spoke those words, or uttered them purposely knowing them to be meaningless, Rostopchin made no reply and hurriedly left him. And strange to say, the Governor of Moscow, the proud Count Rostopchin, picked up a Cossack whip and went to the bridge, where he began shouting and driving away the carts that blocked the way.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: Around four o'clock in the afternoon, Murat's troops were entering Moscow. In front rode a detachment of Wurttemberg hussars, and behind them rode the King of Naples himself, accompanied by a large entourage.

About the middle of Arbat Street, near the Church of the Miraculous Icon of St. Nicholas, Murat halted to await news from the advance detachment about the condition they had found the citadel—the Kremlin—in.
Around Murat gathered a group of those who had remained in Moscow. They all stared in timid bewilderment at the strange, long-haired commander dressed up in feathers and gold.
"Is that their Tsar himself? He's not bad!" low voices could be heard saying.
An interpreter rode up to the group.

"Take off your cap... your caps!" These words went from one to another in the crowd. The interpreter addressed an old porter and asked if it was far to the Kremlin. The porter, listening in perplexity to the unfamiliar Polish accent and not realizing that the interpreter was speaking Russian, did not understand what was being said to him and slipped behind the others.

Murat approached the interpreter and told him to ask where the Russian army was. One of the Russians understood the question, and several voices at once began answering the interpreter. A French officer, returning from the advance detachment, rode up to Murat and reported that the gates of the citadel had been barricaded and that there was probably an ambush there.
"Good!" said Murat, and turning to one of the gentlemen in his suite, ordered four light guns to be moved forward to fire at the gates.

The guns emerged at a trot from the column following Murat and advanced up Arbat Street. When they reached the end of Vozdvizhenka Street, they halted and positioned themselves in the square. Several French officers oversaw the placement of the guns and examined the Kremlin through field glasses.

The bells in the Kremlin were ringing for vespers, and this sound troubled the French. They imagined it to be a call to arms. A few infantrymen ran to the Kutafyev Gate. Beams and wooden screens had been put there, and two musket shots rang out from under the gate as soon as an officer and his men began running toward it. A general standing by the guns shouted orders to the officer, who ran back with his men.
Three more shots came from the gate.

One shot struck a French soldier's foot, and from behind the screens came the strange sound of a few voices shouting. Instantly, as if at a word of command, the expressions of cheerful confidence on the faces of the French general, officers, and men changed to one of determined readiness for combat and suffering. For all of them, from the marshal to the lowest soldier, that place was no longer Vozdvizhenka, Mokhovaya, or Kutafyev Street, nor the Troitsa Gate—familiar places in Moscow—but a new battlefield that would probably prove bloody. And all made ready for that battle. The cries from the gates ceased. The guns were advanced, the artillerymen blew the ash off their fuses, and an officer gave the word "Fire!" This was followed by two whistling rounds of canister shot, one after another. The shot rattled against the stone of the gate and the wooden beams and screens, and two wavering clouds of smoke rose over the square.

A few moments after the echo of the cannon fire resounding over the stone-built Kremlin had died away, the French heard a strange sound above their heads. Thousands of crows rose above the walls and circled in the air, cawing and noisily flapping their wings. Together with that sound came a solitary human cry from the gateway, and through the smoke appeared the figure of a bareheaded man in a peasant's coat. He grasped a musket and took aim at the French. "Fire!" repeated the officer, and the reports of a musket and two cannon shots were heard simultaneously. The gate was again hidden by smoke.

Nothing more moved behind the screens, and the French infantry soldiers and officers advanced to the gate. In the gateway lay three wounded and four dead. Two men in peasant coats ran away at the foot of the wall, toward Znamenka Street.
"Clear that away!" said the officer, pointing to the beams and the corpses, and the French soldiers, after finishing off the wounded, threw the corpses over the parapet.

Who these men were, nobody knew. "Clear that away!" was all that was said of them, and they were thrown over the parapet and removed later so they wouldn't smell. Thiers alone dedicates a few eloquent lines to their memory: "These wretches had occupied the sacred citadel, having armed themselves with guns from the arsenal, and fired" (the wretches) "at the French. Some of them were cut down and the Kremlin was purged of their presence."

Murat was informed that the way had been cleared. The French entered the gates and began setting up camp in the Senate Square. Out of the windows of the Senate House, the soldiers threw chairs into the square for fuel and kindled fires there.

Other detachments passed through the Kremlin and encamped along Moroseyka, Lubyanka, and Pokrovka Streets. Others settled along Vozdvizhenka, Nikolski, and Tverskoy Streets. Finding no homeowners anywhere, the French were not billeted with inhabitants as is usual in towns, but lived in the city as in a military camp.

Though tattered, hungry, worn out, and reduced to a third of their original number, the French entered Moscow in good marching order. It was a weary and famished, but still a fighting and menacing army. But it remained an army only until its soldiers dispersed into their different lodgings. As soon as the men of the various regiments began to spread out among the wealthy, deserted houses, the army was lost forever, and in its place there emerged something that was neither citizens nor soldiers but what are known as marauders. When five weeks later these same men left Moscow, they no longer formed an army. They were a mob of marauders, each carrying a quantity of articles that seemed to him valuable or useful. The aim of each man when he left Moscow was no longer to conquer, but merely to keep what he had acquired. Like a monkey that puts its paw into the narrow neck of a jug, grabs a handful of nuts, and will not open its fist for fear of losing what it holds, and therefore perishes—the French when they left Moscow had inevitably to perish because they carried their loot with them, yet abandoning what they had stolen was as impossible for them as it is for the monkey to let go of its nuts. Ten minutes after each regiment entered a Moscow district, not a soldier or officer was left. Men in military uniforms and Hessian boots could be seen through the windows, laughing and wandering through the rooms. In cellars and storerooms similar men were busy among the provisions, and in the yards they were unlocking or breaking open coach house and stable doors, lighting fires in kitchens, kneading and baking bread with rolled-up sleeves, cooking, or frightening, amusing, or flirting with women and children. There were many such men in both shops and houses—but there was no army.

Order after order was issued by the French commanders that day forbidding the men to disperse about the town, strictly forbidding any violence to the inhabitants or looting, and announcing a roll call for that very evening. But despite all these measures, the men who had until then formed an army flowed all over the wealthy, deserted city with its comforts and plentiful supplies. As a hungry herd of cattle keeps together when crossing a barren field but immediately disperses the moment it reaches rich pastures, so did the army disperse all over the wealthy city.

No residents were left in Moscow, and the soldiers—like water percolating through sand—spread irresistibly through the city in all directions from the Kremlin into which they had first marched. The cavalry, entering a merchant's house that had been abandoned and finding more than enough stabling for their horses, still went on to the next house which seemed better. Many appropriated several houses, chalked their names on them, and quarreled and even fought with other companies for them. Before they had time to secure quarters, the soldiers ran out into the streets to see the city and, hearing that everything had been abandoned, rushed to places where valuables could be had for the taking. The officers followed to stop the soldiers but were themselves drawn into doing the same. In Carriage Row, carriages had been left in the shops, and generals flocked there to select carriages and coaches for themselves. The few inhabitants who had remained invited commanding officers to their houses, hoping to protect themselves from being plundered. There were masses of wealth and there seemed no end to it. All around the quarters occupied by the French were other areas still unexplored and unoccupied where, they thought, even greater riches might be found. And Moscow engulfed the army ever deeper and deeper. When water is spilled on dry ground, both the ground and the water disappear and mud results; in the same way, the entry of the famished army into the rich and deserted city resulted in fires and looting and the destruction of both the army and the wealthy city.

The French attributed the Fire of Moscow to the ferocious patriotism * of Rostopchin; the Russians blamed the barbarity of the French. In reality, however, the burning of Moscow could not be attributed to any individual or any group of people. Moscow burned because it found itself in a position where any town built of wood was bound to burn, quite apart from whether it had a hundred and thirty inferior fire engines or not. Deserted Moscow had to burn as inevitably as a heap of shavings must burn when sparks continuously fall on it for several days. A town built of wood, where fires break out almost daily even when homeowners are present and a police force is maintained, cannot help burning when its inhabitants have left and it is occupied by soldiers who smoke pipes, make campfires of Senate chairs in the Senate Square, and cook themselves meals twice a day. In peacetime, merely billeting troops in the villages of any district immediately increases the number of fires. How much more must the probability of fire increase in an abandoned, wooden town occupied by foreign troops? "The ferocious patriotism of Rostopchin" and the barbarity of the French were not to blame. Moscow was set on fire by soldiers' pipes, kitchens, and campfires, and by the carelessness of enemy soldiers occupying houses they did not own. Even if there was any arson (which is very doubtful, since no one had any reason to burn the houses—in any case a troublesome and dangerous thing to do), arson cannot be regarded as the cause, for the same thing would have happened without it.
* To Rostopchin's ferocious patriotism.

However tempting it might be for the French to blame Rostopchin's ferocity and for the Russians to blame the scoundrel Bonaparte, or later to place a heroic torch in the hands of their own people, it is impossible not to see that there could be no such direct cause of the fire, for Moscow had to burn as every village, factory, or house must burn that is left by its owners and in which strangers are allowed to live and cook their food. Moscow was burned by its inhabitants, it is true, but by those who had abandoned it, not by those who remained in it. Moscow when occupied by the enemy did not remain intact like Berlin, Vienna, and other towns, simply because its inhabitants abandoned it and did not welcome the French with bread and salt, nor bring them the keys of the city.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: The spread of the French through Moscow, radiating outward like a star, only reached the quarter where Pierre was staying by the evening of September second.

After the last two days spent in solitude and unusual circumstances, Pierre was in a state bordering on insanity. He was completely obsessed by one persistent thought. He did not know how or when this thought had taken such possession of him, but he remembered nothing of the past, understood nothing of the present, and all he saw and heard seemed like a dream.

He had left home only to escape the complicated tangle of life's demands that enmeshed him, and which in his present condition he was unable to sort out. He had gone to Joseph Alexeevich's house on the pretext of organizing the deceased's books and papers, but really in search of rest from life's turmoil, for in his mind the memory of Joseph Alexeevich was connected with a world of eternal, solemn, and calm thoughts, quite opposite to the restless confusion into which he felt himself being drawn. He sought a quiet refuge, and in Joseph Alexeevich's study he really found it. When he sat with his elbows on the dusty writing table in the deathlike stillness of the study, calm and significant memories of the last few days rose one after another in his imagination, particularly the battle of Borodino and that vague sense of his own insignificance and insincerity compared with the truth, simplicity, and strength of the class of men he mentally classed as "they." When Gerasim roused him from his reverie, the idea occurred to him of taking part in the popular defense of Moscow, which he knew was being planned. With that aim he had asked Gerasim to get him a peasant's coat and a pistol, and had confided his intention of remaining in Joseph Alexeevich's house and keeping his name secret. Then during the first day spent in inaction and solitude (he tried several times to concentrate on the Masonic manuscripts but couldn't), the idea that had previously occurred to him of the cabalistic significance of his name in connection with Bonaparte's more than once vaguely presented itself. But the idea that he, L'russe Besuhof, was destined to set a limit to the power of the Beast was as yet only one of those fancies that often passed through his mind and left no trace.

When, having bought the coat merely to take part among the people in the defense of Moscow, Pierre had met the Rostovs and Natasha had said to him: "Are you remaining in Moscow?... How wonderful!" the thought flashed into his mind that it really would be a good thing, even if Moscow were taken, for him to remain there and do what he was predestined to do.

The next day, focused solely on not sparing himself and not lagging behind anyone, Pierre went to the Three Hills gate. But when he returned to the house, convinced that Moscow would not be defended, he suddenly felt that what had previously seemed merely a possibility had now become absolutely necessary and inevitable. He must remain in Moscow, conceal his name, meet Napoleon, and kill him—either perishing himself or putting an end to the misery of all Europe, which seemed to him entirely due to Napoleon.

Pierre knew all the details of the attempt on Bonaparte's life in 1809 by a German student in Vienna, and knew that the student had been shot. And the risk to which he would expose his own life by carrying out his plan excited him still more.

Two equally powerful feelings drew Pierre irresistibly to this purpose. The first was a feeling of the necessity of sacrifice and suffering in view of the common calamity—the same feeling that had caused him to go to Mozhaysk on the twenty-fifth and to plunge into the very thick of the battle, and had now caused him to run away from home and, in place of the luxury and comfort he was accustomed to, to sleep on a hard sofa without undressing and eat the same food as Gerasim. The other was that vague and distinctly Russian feeling of contempt for everything conventional, artificial, and human—for everything the majority of men regard as the greatest good in the world. Pierre had first experienced this strange and fascinating feeling at the Sloboda Palace, when he had suddenly felt that wealth, power, and life—all that men so painstakingly acquire and guard—if it has any worth, has so only by reason of the joy with which it can all be renounced.

It was the feeling that makes a volunteer recruit spend his last penny on drink, and a drunken man smash mirrors or glasses for no apparent reason, knowing it will cost him everything he owns: the feeling which causes a man to do things that from an ordinary point of view are insane, as if to test his personal power and strength, affirming the existence of a higher, nonhuman standard of life.

From the very day Pierre had first experienced this feeling at the Sloboda Palace, he had been continuously under its influence, but only now did he find full satisfaction for it. Moreover, at this moment Pierre was sustained in his plan, and prevented from giving it up, by what he had already done in that direction. If he were now to leave Moscow like everyone else, his flight from home, the peasant coat, the pistol, and his announcement to the Rostovs that he would remain in Moscow would all become not merely meaningless but contemptible and ridiculous—and Pierre was very sensitive to that.

Pierre's physical condition, as is always the case, matched his mental state. The unaccustomed coarse food, the vodka he drank during those days, the absence of wine and cigars, his dirty unchanged linen, two almost sleepless nights on a short sofa without bedding—all this kept him in a state of excitement bordering on insanity.

It was two o'clock in the afternoon. The French had already entered Moscow. Pierre knew this, but instead of acting he only thought about his undertaking, going over its smallest details in his mind. In his imagination, he did not clearly picture the striking of the blow or the death of Napoleon, but with extraordinary vividness and melancholy pleasure imagined his own destruction and heroic endurance.

"Yes, alone, for the sake of all, I must do it or die!" he thought. "Yes, I will approach... and then suddenly... with pistol or dagger? But that doesn't matter! 'It is not I but the hand of Providence that punishes you,' I shall say," thought he, imagining what he would say when killing Napoleon. "Well then, take me and execute me!" he went on, speaking to himself and bowing his head with a sad but determined expression.

While Pierre, standing in the middle of the room, was talking to himself this way, the study door opened and on the threshold appeared the figure of Makar Alexeevich, always so timid before but now quite transformed.

His dressing gown was unfastened, his face red and distorted. He was obviously drunk. Seeing Pierre, he was confused at first, but noticing Pierre's own embarrassment, he immediately grew bold and, staggering on his thin legs, advanced into the middle of the room.
"They're frightened," he said in a hoarse, confidential voice. "I say I won't surrender, I say... Am I not right, sir?"
He paused, then suddenly seeing the pistol on the table, seized it with unexpected speed and ran out into the corridor.

Gerasim and the porter, who had followed Makar Alexeevich, stopped him in the vestibule and tried to take the pistol from him. Pierre, coming out into the corridor, looked with pity and revulsion at the half-crazy old man. Makar Alexeevich, straining with effort, held on to the pistol and screamed hoarsely, evidently with some heroic fantasy in his head.
"To arms! Board them! No, you shan't have it!" he yelled.
"That will do, please, that will do. Have the goodness—please, sir, to let go! Please, sir..." pleaded Gerasim, trying carefully to steer Makar Alexeevich by the elbows back to the door.
"Who are you? Bonaparte!..." shouted Makar Alexeevich.
"That's not right, sir. Come to your room, please, and rest. Allow me to have the pistol."
"Get away, you vile slave! Don't touch me! See this?" shouted Makar Alexeevich, brandishing the pistol. "Board them!"
"Grab him!" whispered Gerasim to the porter.
They seized Makar Alexeevich by the arms and dragged him to the door.
The vestibule filled with the discordant sounds of a struggle and a tipsy, hoarse voice.
Suddenly a fresh sound—a piercing feminine scream—rang out from the porch, and the cook came running into the vestibule.
"It's them! Lord have mercy! O Lord, four of them, horsemen!" she cried.
Gerasim and the porter let Makar Alexeevich go, and in the now silent corridor the sound of several hands knocking at the front door could be heard.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Pierre, having decided that until he carried out his plan he would reveal neither his identity nor his knowledge of French, stood at the half-open corridor door, intending to hide as soon as the French entered. But the French came in, and still Pierre did not retreat—an irresistible curiosity kept him there.

There were two of them. One was an officer—a tall, soldierly, handsome man—the other evidently a private or an orderly, sunburned, short, and thin, with sunken cheeks and a dull expression. The officer walked in front, leaning on a stick and limping slightly. When he had advanced a few steps, he stopped, apparently having decided these were good quarters, turned to the soldiers standing at the entrance, and in a loud voice ordered them to stable the horses. Having done that, the officer, lifting his elbow with a smart gesture, stroked his mustache and lightly touched his hat.
"Good day, everybody!" he said gaily, smiling and looking about him.
* "Good day, everybody!"
No one answered.
"Are you the master here?" the officer asked Gerasim.
* "Are you the master here?"
Gerasim gazed at the officer with an alarmed and questioning look.

"Quarters, quarters, lodgings!" said the officer, looking down at the little man with a condescending, good-natured smile. "The French are good fellows. Come now! Don't let's be cross, old fellow!" he added, clapping the scared and silent Gerasim on the shoulder. "Well, does no one speak French in this establishment?" he asked again in French, looking around and meeting Pierre's eyes. Pierre moved away from the door.
* "Quarters, quarters, lodgings! The French are good fellows. What the devil! There, don't let us be cross, old fellow!"
Again the officer turned to Gerasim and asked him to show him the rooms in the house.
"Master, not here—don't understand... me, you..." said Gerasim, trying to make his words more comprehensible by distorting them.

Still smiling, the French officer spread out his hands before Gerasim's nose, indicating that he didn't understand him either, and moved, limping, to the door where Pierre was standing. Pierre wanted to go away and hide, but at that moment he saw Makar Alexeevich appearing at the open kitchen door with the pistol in his hand. With a madman's cunning, Makar Alexeevich eyed the Frenchman, raised his pistol, and took aim.

"Board them!" yelled the tipsy man, trying to pull the trigger. Hearing the yell, the officer turned around, and at the same moment Pierre threw himself at the drunkard. Just as Pierre grabbed and knocked up the pistol, Makar Alexeevich finally got his fingers on the trigger—there was a deafening report, and everything was enveloped in a cloud of smoke. The Frenchman turned pale and rushed to the door.
Forgetting his intention of concealing his knowledge of French, Pierre snatched away the pistol, threw it down, ran up to the officer, and addressed him in French.
"You are not wounded?" he asked.

"I think not," answered the Frenchman, feeling himself over. "But I've had a lucky escape this time," he added, pointing to the damaged plaster on the wall. "Who is that man?" he asked, looking sternly at Pierre.
"Oh, I am truly sorry about what has happened," said Pierre quickly, completely forgetting the role he had meant to play. "He is an unfortunate madman who did not know what he was doing."
The officer went up to Makar Alexeevich and took him by the collar.
Makar Alexeevich was standing with parted lips, swaying as if about to fall asleep, leaning against the wall.

"Scoundrel! You shall pay for this," said the Frenchman, letting go of him. "We French are merciful after victory, but we do not pardon traitors," he added, with a look of gloomy dignity and a fine, dramatic gesture.

Pierre continued, in French, to persuade the officer not to hold the drunken imbecile accountable. The Frenchman listened in silence with the same gloomy expression, but suddenly turned to Pierre with a smile. For a few seconds he looked at him in silence. His handsome face assumed a melodramatically gentle expression and he held out his hand.
"You have saved my life. You are French," said he.

For a Frenchman, that conclusion was indisputable. Only a Frenchman could perform a great deed, and to save his life—the life of Monsieur Ramballe, captain of the 13th Light Regiment—was undoubtedly a very great deed.
But however certain that conclusion and the officer's conviction based upon it, Pierre felt it necessary to correct him.
"I am Russian," he said quickly.

"Oh, come now! Tell that to others," said the officer, waving his finger before his nose and smiling. "You shall tell me all about that later. I am delighted to meet a compatriot. Well, and what are we to do with this man?" he added, addressing Pierre as a brother.

Even if Pierre were not a Frenchman, having once received that loftiest of human titles, he could not renounce it—the officer's look and tone said as much. In reply to his last question, Pierre again explained who Makar Alexeevich was and how just before their arrival the drunken imbecile had seized the loaded pistol which they had not had time to take from him, and he begged the officer to let the deed go unpunished.
The Frenchman puffed out his chest and made a grand gesture with his arm.

"You have saved my life! You are French. You ask his pardon? I grant it. Lead that man away!" he said quickly and energetically, and taking the arm of Pierre—whom he had promoted to the status of Frenchman for saving his life—he went with him into the room.
The soldiers in the yard, hearing the shot, came into the corridor asking what had happened, and expressed their readiness to punish the culprit, but the officer sternly stopped them.
"You will be called when you are wanted," he said.
The soldiers went out again, and the orderly, who had meanwhile had time to visit the kitchen, came up to his officer.
"Captain, there is soup and a leg of mutton in the kitchen," said he. "Shall I serve them up?"
"Yes, and some wine," answered the captain.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 29
paragraphs: When the French officer went into the room with Pierre, the latter again thought it his duty to assure him that he was not French and wished to leave, but the officer would not hear of it. He was so polite, friendly, good-natured, and genuinely grateful to Pierre for saving his life that Pierre couldn't bring himself to refuse, and sat down with him in the parlor—the first room they entered. To Pierre's insistence that he was not a Frenchman, the captain, evidently unable to understand how anyone could decline so flattering a designation, shrugged his shoulders and said that if Pierre absolutely insisted on passing for a Russian, so be it, but that he would be forever bound to Pierre by gratitude for saving his life.

Had this man been capable of even slightly perceiving the feelings of others, and had he at all understood what Pierre's feelings were, Pierre would probably have left him. But the man's oblivious self-absorption disarmed Pierre.

"A Frenchman or a Russian prince incognito," said the officer, looking at Pierre's fine though dirty linen and at the ring on his finger. "I owe my life to you and offer you my friendship. A Frenchman never forgets either an insult or a service. I offer you my friendship. That is all I can say."

There was so much good nature and nobility (in the French sense of the word) in the officer's voice, in the expression of his face, and in his gestures, that Pierre, unconsciously smiling in response to the Frenchman's smile, shook the hand held out to him.

"Captain Ramballe, of the 13th Light Regiment, Chevalier of the Legion of Honor for the affair on the seventh of September," he introduced himself, a self-satisfied, irrepressible smile puckering his lips under his mustache. "Will you now be so good as to tell me with whom I have the honor of conversing so pleasantly, instead of being in the field hospital with that maniac's bullet in my body?"
Pierre replied that he could not tell him his name and, blushing, began to try to invent a name and explain his reason for concealing it, but the Frenchman hastily interrupted him.

"Oh, please!" said he. "I understand your reasons. You are an officer... a superior officer perhaps. You have borne arms against us. That's not my business. I owe you my life. That is enough for me. I am entirely at your service. You belong to the gentry?" he concluded with a shade of inquiry in his tone. Pierre bent his head. "Your first name, if you please. That is all I ask. Monsieur Pierre, you say?... That's all I want to know."

When the mutton and an omelet had been served and a samovar and vodka brought, along with some wine which the French had taken from a Russian cellar, Ramballe invited Pierre to share his dinner and immediately began eating greedily and quickly like a healthy, hungry man, chewing his food rapidly with his strong teeth, continually smacking his lips and repeating: "Excellent! Delicious!" His face grew red and was covered with sweat. Pierre was hungry and shared the dinner with pleasure. Morel, the orderly, brought some hot water in a saucepan and placed a bottle of claret in it. He also brought a bottle of kvass from the kitchen for them to try. That drink was already known to the French and had been given a special name. They called it "pig's lemonade," and Morel spoke well of the pig's lemonade he had found in the kitchen. But since the captain had the wine they had taken while passing through Moscow, he left the kvass to Morel and turned to the bottle of Bordeaux. He wrapped the bottle up to its neck in a napkin and poured out wine for himself and for Pierre. The satisfaction of his hunger and the wine made the captain still livelier, and he chatted nonstop all through dinner.

"Yes, my dear Monsieur Pierre, I owe you a fine votive candle for saving me from that maniac... You see, I've got enough bullets in my body already. Here is one I got at Wagram" (he touched his side) "and a second at Smolensk"—he showed a scar on his cheek—"and this leg which as you see doesn't want to cooperate, I got that on the seventh at the great battle of la Moskowa. Good Lord! It was splendid! That storm of fire was worth seeing. It was a tough job you set us there, I must say! You may be proud of it! And on my honor, despite the cough I caught there, I'd be ready to do it all over again. I pity those who missed it."
"I was there," said Pierre.

"Really? So much the better! You are certainly brave enemies. The great redoubt held out well, by my word!" continued the Frenchman. "And you made us pay dearly for it. I was at it three times—I swear it. Three times we reached the guns and three times we were thrown back like cardboard figures. Oh, it was magnificent, Monsieur Pierre! Your grenadiers were superb, by heaven! I saw them close up their ranks six times in a row and march as if on parade. Wonderful men! Our King of Naples, who knows what's what, cried 'Bravo!' Ha, ha! So you are one of us soldiers!" he added, smiling, after a momentary pause. "So much the better, so much the better, Monsieur Pierre! Terrible in battle... gallant with the ladies" (he winked and smiled), "that's what the French are, Monsieur Pierre, isn't it?"

The captain was so naturally and good-humoredly cheerful, so genuine, and so pleased with himself that Pierre almost winked back as he looked merrily at him. Probably the word "gallant" turned the captain's thoughts to the state of Moscow.
"By the way, tell me, is it true that the women have all left Moscow? What a strange idea! What did they have to be afraid of?"
"Would not the French ladies leave Paris if the Russians entered it?" asked Pierre.
"Ha, ha, ha!" The Frenchman let out a merry, hearty chuckle, patting Pierre on the shoulder. "What a thing to say!" he exclaimed. "Paris?... But Paris, Paris..."
"Paris—the capital of the world," Pierre finished for him.
The captain looked at Pierre. He had a habit of stopping short in the middle of his talk and gazing intently with his laughing, kindly eyes.
"Well, if you hadn't told me you were Russian, I would have bet you were Parisian! You have that certain something, that..." and having paid this compliment, he again gazed at Pierre in silence.
"I have been in Paris. I spent years there," said Pierre.

"Oh yes, one can tell. Paris! A man who doesn't know Paris is a savage. You can spot a Parisian two leagues away. Paris is Talma, la Duchenois, Potier, the Sorbonne, the boulevards," and noticing that his conclusion was weaker than what had come before, he added quickly: "There is only one Paris in the world. You have been to Paris and have remained Russian. Well, I don't think any less of you for it."
Under the influence of the wine and after the days spent alone with his depressing thoughts, Pierre involuntarily enjoyed talking with this cheerful, good-natured man.

"To return to your ladies—I hear they are beautiful. What a foolish idea to go bury themselves in the steppes when the French army is in Moscow. What a chance those girls have missed! Your peasants—that's another matter; but you civilized people ought to know us better. We took Vienna, Berlin, Madrid, Naples, Rome, Warsaw—all the world's capitals. We are feared, but we are loved. We are good to know. And then the Emperor..." he began, but Pierre interrupted him.
"The Emperor," Pierre repeated, and his face suddenly became sad and embarrassed. "Is the Emperor...?"

"The Emperor? He is generosity, mercy, justice, order, genius—that's what the Emperor is! It is I, Ramballe, who tell you so... I assure you I was his enemy eight years ago. My father was an emigrant count... But that man has won me over. He seized hold of me. I could not resist the sight of the grandeur and glory with which he has covered France. When I understood what he wanted—when I saw that he was preparing a bed of laurels for us—I said to myself: 'That is a monarch,' and I devoted myself to him! And so there it is! Oh yes, my dear friend, he is the greatest man of the ages past or future."
"Is he in Moscow?" Pierre asked with a guilty look.
The Frenchman looked at his guilty face and smiled.
"No, he will make his entry tomorrow," he replied, and continued his talk.

Their conversation was interrupted by cries of several voices at the gate and by Morel, who came to say that some Wurttemberg hussars had arrived and wanted to put their horses in the yard where the captain's horses were. This difficulty had arisen mainly because the hussars did not understand what was being said to them in French.

The captain had their senior sergeant called in and in a stern voice asked him what regiment he belonged to, who his commanding officer was, and by what right he allowed himself to claim quarters that were already occupied. The German, who knew little French, answered the first two questions by giving the names of his regiment and commanding officer, but in reply to the third—which he did not understand—said, mixing broken French into his German, that he was the quartermaster of the regiment and his commander had ordered him to occupy all the houses one after another. Pierre, who knew German, translated what the German said to the captain and gave the captain's reply to the Wurttemberg hussar in German. When the German understood what was being said, he submitted and took his men elsewhere. The captain went out onto the porch and gave some orders in a loud voice.

When he returned to the room, Pierre was sitting in the same place as before, with his head in his hands. His face showed suffering. He really was suffering at that moment. When the captain went out and Pierre was left alone, he suddenly came to his senses and realized the position he was in. It was not that Moscow had been taken or that the happy conquerors were masters in it and patronizing him. Painful as that was, it was not what tormented Pierre. He was tormented by the consciousness of his own weakness. The few glasses of wine he had drunk and the conversation with this good-natured man had destroyed the mood of concentrated gloom in which he had spent the last few days, and which was essential for carrying out his plan. The pistol, dagger, and peasant coat were ready. Napoleon was to enter the city the next day. Pierre still believed it would be useful and worthy to kill the tyrant, but now he felt he would not do it. He did not know why, but sensed that he would not carry out his intention. He struggled against admitting his weakness but dimly felt that he could not overcome it, and that his former dark mood—concerning vengeance, killing, and self-sacrifice—had been scattered like dust by contact with the first man he met.
The captain returned to the room, limping slightly and whistling a tune.

The Frenchman's chatter, which had previously amused Pierre, now repelled him. The tune he was whistling, his walk, and the gesture with which he twirled his mustache all now seemed offensive. "I will leave immediately. I won't say another word to him," thought Pierre. He thought this, but still sat in the same spot. A strange feeling of weakness held him there; he wanted to get up and leave, but could not.
The captain, on the other hand, seemed very cheerful. He paced up and down the room twice. His eyes shone and his mustache twitched as if he were smiling to himself at some amusing thought.

"The colonel of those Wurttembergers is delightful," he suddenly said. "He's a German, but a nice fellow all the same... But he's a German." He sat down facing Pierre. "By the way, you speak German then?"
Pierre looked at him in silence.
"What is the German for 'shelter'?"
"Shelter?" Pierre repeated. "The German for shelter is Unterkunft."
"How do you say it?" the captain asked quickly and doubtfully.
"Unterkunft," Pierre repeated.
"Onterkoff," said the captain, and looked at Pierre for some seconds with laughing eyes. "These Germans are first-rate fools, don't you think so, Monsieur Pierre?" he concluded.
"Well, let's have another bottle of this Moscow Bordeaux, shall we? Morel will warm us up another little bottle. Morel!" he called out cheerfully.

Morel brought candles and a bottle of wine. The captain looked at Pierre by the candlelight and was evidently struck by the troubled expression on his companion's face. Ramballe, with genuine concern and sympathy in his face, went up to Pierre and bent over him.
"Come now, we're sad," said he, touching Pierre's hand. "Have I upset you? No, really, have you anything against me?" he asked. "Perhaps it's the state of affairs?"
Pierre did not answer but looked warmly into the Frenchman's eyes, whose expression of sympathy was pleasing to him.

"Honestly, without speaking of what I owe you, I feel friendship for you. Can I do anything for you? Count on me. It is for life and death. I say it with my hand on my heart!" said he, striking his chest.
"Thank you," said Pierre.
The captain gazed intently at him as he had done when learning that "shelter" was Unterkunft in German, and his face suddenly brightened.
"Well, in that case, I drink to our friendship!" he cried gaily, filling two glasses with wine.
Pierre took one of the glasses and emptied it. Ramballe emptied his too, pressed Pierre's hand again, and leaned his elbows on the table in a pensive attitude.

"Yes, my dear friend," he began, "such are the twists of fortune. Who would have said that I would be a soldier and a captain of dragoons in the service of Bonaparte, as we used to call him? Yet here I am in Moscow with him. I must tell you, my dear friend," he continued in the sad and measured tones of a man who intends to tell a long story, "that our family name is one of the most ancient in France."

And with a Frenchman's easy and natural frankness, the captain told Pierre the story of his ancestors, his childhood, youth, and manhood, and all about his relatives and his financial and family affairs, with "my poor mother" playing of course an important part in the story.
"But all that is only life's setting; the real thing is love—love! Am I not right, Monsieur Pierre?" said he, growing animated. "Another glass?"
Pierre again emptied his glass and poured himself a third.
"Oh, women, women!" and the captain, looking with glistening eyes at Pierre, began talking about love and his love affairs.

There were very many of these, as one could easily believe looking at the officer's handsome, self-satisfied face and noting the eager enthusiasm with which he spoke of women. Though all of Ramballe's love stories had the sensual character which Frenchmen regard as the special charm and poetry of love, he told his story with such sincere conviction that he alone had experienced and known all love's charm, and he described women so enticingly, that Pierre listened to him with curiosity.

It was clear that the kind of love the Frenchman was so fond of was not the low, simple kind that Pierre had once felt for his wife, nor the romantic love, fueled by his own imagination, that he had experienced for Natasha. (Ramballe despised both of these equally: one he called the "love of peasants" and the other the "love of simpletons.") The love the Frenchman worshiped consisted mainly in the artificiality of his relations with women and in a combination of absurdities that gave the feeling its chief appeal.

Thus the captain touchingly recounted the story of his love for a fascinating marquise of thirty-five and at the same time for a charming, innocent child of seventeen—the bewitching marquise's daughter. The conflict of generosity between mother and daughter, ending in the mother sacrificing herself and offering her daughter in marriage to her lover, still moved the captain, though it was a distant memory. Then he recounted an episode in which the husband played the part of the lover and he—the lover—assumed the role of the husband, as well as several amusing incidents from his time in Germany, where "shelter" is called Unterkunft and where the husbands eat sauerkraut and the young girls are "too blonde."

Finally, the most recent episode—in Poland, still fresh in the captain's memory—which he narrated with rapid gestures and a glowing face, was of how he had saved the life of a Pole (in general, the saving of lives continually occurred in the captain's stories) and the Pole had entrusted to him his enchanting wife (a Parisian at heart) while himself entering the French service. The captain was happy, the enchanting Polish lady wished to elope with him, but, prompted by noble feeling, the captain restored the wife to the husband, saying as he did so: "I have saved your life, and I save your honor!" Having repeated these words, the captain wiped his eyes and gave himself a shake, as if driving away the weakness that overcame him at this touching recollection.

Listening to the captain's tales, Pierre—as often happens late in the evening and under the influence of wine—followed all that was told him, understood it all, and at the same time followed a train of personal memories that, he knew not why, suddenly arose in his mind. While listening to these love stories, his own love for Natasha unexpectedly surfaced, and going over the images of that love in his imagination, he mentally compared them with Ramballe's tales. Listening to the story of the struggle between love and duty, Pierre saw before his eyes every tiny detail of his last meeting with the object of his love at the Sukharev water tower. At the time, that meeting had not made an impact on him—he had not even once recalled it. But now it seemed to him that there had been something very important and poetic in it.

"Peter Kirilovich, come here! We recognized you," he now seemed to hear the words she had spoken and to see before him her eyes, her smile, her traveling hood, and a stray lock of her hair... and there seemed to him something deeply touching in all of this.

Having finished his tale about the enchanting Polish lady, the captain asked Pierre if he had ever experienced a similar urge to sacrifice himself for love and a feeling of envy of the legitimate husband.

Prompted by this question, Pierre raised his head and felt a need to express the thoughts that filled his mind. He began to explain that he understood love for a woman somewhat differently. He said that in all his life he had loved and still loved only one woman, and that she could never be his.
"Really!" said the captain.

Pierre then explained that he had loved this woman from his earliest years, but had not dared to think of her because she was too young, and because he had been an illegitimate son without a name. Later, when he had received a name and wealth, he dared not think of her because he loved her too much, placing her far above everything in the world, and especially therefore above himself.
When he had reached this point, Pierre asked the captain whether he understood that.
The captain made a gesture suggesting that even if he did not understand it, he begged Pierre to continue.
"Platonic love, clouds..." he muttered.

Whether it was the wine he had drunk, or an impulse of frankness, or the thought that this man did not and never would know any of those who played a part in his story, or whether it was all these things together, something loosened Pierre's tongue. Speaking thickly and with a faraway look in his shining eyes, he told the whole story of his life: his marriage, Natasha's love for his best friend, her betrayal of him, and all his own simple relations with her. Urged on by Ramballe's questions, he also told what he had first kept hidden—his own position, and even his name.

More than anything else in Pierre's story, the captain was impressed by the fact that Pierre was very rich, had two mansions in Moscow, and that he had abandoned everything and not left the city, but remained there concealing his name and station.

When it was late at night they went out together into the street. The night was warm and light. To the left of the house on Pokrovka, a fire glowed—the first of those that were beginning in Moscow. To the right and high up in the sky hung the sickle of the waning moon, and opposite it hung that bright comet which was connected in Pierre's heart with his love. At the gate stood Gerasim, the cook, and two Frenchmen. Their laughter and their mutually incomprehensible remarks in two languages could be heard. They were looking at the glow in the town.
There was nothing frightening about the one small, distant fire in the immense city.

Gazing at the high starry sky, at the moon, at the comet, and at the glow from the fire, Pierre felt a rush of joyful emotion. "There now, how good it is, what more does one need?" thought he. And suddenly, remembering his plan, he grew dizzy and felt so faint that he leaned against the fence to keep from falling.
Without taking leave of his new friend, Pierre left the gate with unsteady steps and, returning to his room, lay down on the sofa and immediately fell asleep.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 30
paragraphs: The glow of the first fire that began on the second of September was watched from the various roads by the fleeing Muscovites and by the retreating troops, with many different feelings.

The Rostov family spent the night at Mytishchi, fourteen miles from Moscow. They had started so late on the first of September, the road had been so blocked by vehicles and troops, and so many things had been forgotten and servants sent back for them, that they decided to spend that night at a place just three miles outside Moscow. The next morning they woke late and were again delayed so often that they only got as far as Great Mytishchi. At ten o'clock that evening, the Rostov family and the wounded traveling with them were all distributed in the yards and huts of that large village. The Rostovs' servants and coachmen and the orderlies of the wounded officers, after seeing to their masters, had supper, fed the horses, and came out onto the porches.

In a neighboring hut lay Raevsky's adjutant with a fractured wrist. The terrible pain he suffered made him moan constantly and pitifully, and his moaning sounded dreadful in the darkness of the autumn night. He had spent the first night in the same yard as the Rostovs. The countess said she had been unable to close her eyes because of his moaning, and at Mytishchi she moved to a worse hut simply to be farther from the wounded man.

In the darkness of the night one of the servants noticed, above the high body of a coach standing before the porch, the small glow of another fire. One glow had long been visible and everybody knew it was Little Mytishchi burning—set on fire by Mamonov's Cossacks.
"But look here, brothers, there's another fire!" remarked an orderly.
All turned their attention to the glow.
"But they told us Little Mytishchi was set on fire by Mamonov's Cossacks."
"But that's not Mytishchi, it's farther away."
"Look, it must be in Moscow!"
Two of those watching went around to the other side of the coach and sat down on its steps.
"It's more to the left. Why, Little Mytishchi is over there, and this is right on the other side."
Several men joined the first two.
"See how it's flaring," said one. "That's a fire in Moscow: either in the Sushchevsky or the Rogozhsky quarter."
No one replied, and for some time they all gazed silently at the spreading flames of the second fire in the distance.
Old Daniel Terentich, the count's valet (as he was called), came up to the group and shouted at Mishka.
"What are you staring at, you good-for-nothing?... The count will be calling and there's nobody there; go and gather the clothes together."
"I only ran out to get some water," said Mishka.
"But what do you think, Daniel Terentich? Doesn't it look as if that glow is in Moscow?" remarked one of the footmen.
Daniel Terentich made no reply, and again for a long time they were all silent. The glow spread, rising and falling, farther and farther.
"God have mercy... It's windy and dry..." said another voice.
"Just look! See what it's doing now. O Lord! You can even see the crows flying. Lord have mercy on us sinners!"
"They'll put it out, don't worry!"

"Who's going to put it out?" Daniel Terentich, who had been silent till then, was heard to say. His voice was calm and deliberate. "Moscow it is, brothers," said he. "Mother Moscow, the white..." his voice faltered, and he gave way to an old man's sob.
And it was as if they had all only been waiting for this to understand the significance of the glow they were watching. Sighs were heard, words of prayer, and the sobbing of the count's old valet.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 31
paragraphs: The valet, returning to the cottage, told the count that Moscow was burning. The count put on his dressing gown and went out to look. Sonya and Madame Schoss, who had not yet undressed, went out with him. Only Natasha and the countess remained in the room. Petya was no longer with the family—he had gone on with his regiment, which was heading for Troitsa.

The countess, hearing that Moscow was on fire, began to cry. Natasha, pale and with a fixed look, was sitting on the bench under the icons just where she had sat down on arriving, and paid no attention to her father's words. She was listening to the ceaseless moaning of the adjutant, three houses away.
